grade.first_issue: The claimed eventual stabilization of \(\mathcal G_n\) does not follow from the preceding argument. Although every minimal hitting set \(H\) lies in \(\bigcup\mathcal G_n\), the set actually added is \(S_{n+1}=H^*\cup\mathcal P(k)\), which may introduce new primes and be incomparable with every old member; thus there is no fixed finite universe and no demonstrated decreasing process.
grade.summary: The solution correctly reformulates admissibility using hitting sets and gives a valid periodicity argument conditional on eventual stabilization of the minimal prime-support family. However, stabilization is the central finiteness theorem of the problem, and the submitted justification for it is invalid. The new support is not generally a minimal hitting set and may contain arbitrarily new prime factors, so the asserted finite-state argument cannot be applied. Establishing stabilization requires a substantially new, load-bearing finiteness argument. Under the mandatory cap for an unjustified decisive inference replacing the central argument, the proof merits 3.
strengths: Correctly translates the gcd conditions into a hitting-set formulation.
The argument that \(\mathcal G_n\) remains intersecting is essentially correct despite imprecise wording about its updated members.
The formula expressing the next admissible integer through minimal hitting sets is sound.
Once a finite stabilized family is assumed, the congruence-periodicity and consecutive-enumeration argument is substantially correct.

errors.description: The proof of eventual stabilization is invalid: finiteness of the subsets of the stage-dependent set \(\bigcup\mathcal G_n\) gives no global bound, because subsequent supports can introduce new primes through the quotient \(k\).

The statement that the process adds minimal hitting sets and replaces elements by smaller sets misdescribes the process. It adds \(S_{n+1}\), which may strictly contain \(H^*\), may be incomparable with all existing members, and may enlarge rather than decrease the minimal family.

Several later claims, including that every \(S_k\) contains a member of the limiting family and that hitting the limit implies hitting every earlier \(\mathcal G_n\), are asserted without proof; they would follow only after a valid stabilization-and-containment argument.
